newsitem.title: Mexico: Strong quake rocks central, western Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Strong quake rocks central, western Mexico.

text.p: A strong earthquake shook western and central Mexico on Saturday afternoon, sending people running out into the streets in panic but causing no apparent major damage in the capital.
"I was watching television and everything began to shake," said Luis Garcia, an office cleaner in Mexico City. "Suddenly, it rocked violently. It felt terrible."

Private radio station Radio Red quoted Mexico's National Earthquake Centre as saying the quake measured 7.3 on the Richter scale. "It's a big quake and it lasted a long time," said centre spokesman Carlos Fuentes.
The U.S. Geological Survey in Golden, Colorado said it had made a preliminary estimate of 6.8 for the quake's strength, though this could change.

The tremor's epicentre was under the Pacific Ocean 30 miles (50 km) west-northwest of Playa Azul, Michoacan state, a survey spokesman said. This was in a fairly sparsely populated area about 250 miles (410 km) southwest of Mexico City.
The quake hit Mexico City at around 2:30 p.m. local time (2030 GMT) and was felt all over the city, as well as in at least seven states of central and western Mexico.
Some small objects fell from shelves in houses in the capital, car alarms went off, traffic screeched to a halt, and panicked residents fled to the streets for safety.
Radio reports said at least two large public buildings suffered cracks in them but no major structural damage.
Witnesses also said the quake was felt strongly in Michoacan state and in tourist resorts along the Pacific coast in the neighbouring state of Guerrero.
Louis Lichtenstein, a U.S. tourist from Minnesota, told Reuters by telephone from the resort of Ixtapa that the tremor was the strongest he had ever felt.
"The earth shook in a rotational manner with some hard shocks, " he said. "We were very glad to be sitting in an open-air restaurant and not in the hotel."
Miguel Borrego, a Michocan state official, told reporters 80 percent of the residents in the state's port of Lazaro Cardenas were without water or electricity because of the quake.
He had no other immediate reports of damage, but noted that it had not been possible to check with some remote towns because communications had been knocked out.

Roberto Mestizo, a reporter with the La Opinion de Michoacan newspaper, said in an interview by telephone from the town of Uruapan that the quake caused "a lot of panic" but as far as he knew no major damage and no apparent victims.
The Red Cross in Mexico City said it had no reports of injuries or damage from the quake there.
The tremor was also felt in Mexico's second city of Guadalajara, although residents said there were no immediate signs of damage.

Much of Mexico lies along a geological fault line and feels small earthquakes regularly. The last strong quake to hit Mexico was on July 15 last year, when a tremor measuring 6.5 on the Richter scale struck southern Mexico, causing panic but no injuries.
Central areas of Mexico City were destroyed by two huge quakes in September 1985, the larger of which measured a massive 8.1 on the Richter scale.
